title: Reorganize String
description: Brute force to optimized: searching permutations versus a feasibility check plus a greedy max-heap construction that avoids adjacent repeats.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a string s, rearrange its characters so that no two adjacent characters are the same. Return any valid rearrangement, or an empty string if no valid rearrangement exists.

blocks.text: Rearrange the characters of s so that no two identical characters end up next to each other, if such an arrangement is possible at all.

blocks.title: Analogy: Seating Guests So No Two From the Same Group Sit Together
blocks.text: Picture seating people from different groups in a row, needing to avoid ever placing two people from the same group next to each other. Always seating the LARGEST remaining group next (as long as it wasn't just seated) spreads that group out as evenly as possible.

blocks.caption: If the most frequent character exceeds ceil(n/2), no valid arrangement exists

blocks.text: One valid rearrangement is "aba", with no two adjacent characters equal.
The character 'a' appears 3 times in a string of length 4, exceeding ceil(4/2) = 2, so no valid arrangement exists, and the answer is an empty string.

Before searching through permutations, notice that a simple frequency check determines feasibility immediately, and a greedy "always place the most frequent remaining character" strategy builds a valid arrangement directly when one exists.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If any character appears more than ceil(n/2) times, it cannot be spread out enough to avoid at least one adjacent repeat, making the task impossible.

Observation 2: When that condition is not violated, greedily placing the currently most frequent remaining character at each position (as long as it was not the character just placed) always succeeds in building a valid arrangement.

Observation 3: A max-heap, ordered by remaining count, gives direct access to the currently most frequent character at every step.

Observation 4: If the top of the heap is the character just placed, temporarily set it aside and use the SECOND most frequent character instead, then return the first back to the heap.
This leads to a feasibility check followed by a greedy max-heap construction, always placing the most frequent remaining character that was not just used.
Conceptually, try every permutation of the string's characters, checking each for the no-adjacent-repeats property, and return the first valid one found.

items: Generate every distinct permutation of the characters in s.
Check each permutation for any two adjacent equal characters.
Return the first valid permutation found, or an empty string if none exists.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every distinct arrangement of the characters is generated and checked directly for the no-adjacent-repeats property.
This is only feasible for extremely short strings, with up to 500 characters it is entirely impractical.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: factorial in the string length, generating every permutation.
Space: O(n!) in the worst case to store distinct permutations.
Limitation: generating permutations is entirely impractical beyond a handful of characters; a direct feasibility check plus greedy construction avoids searching altogether.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why permutation search is unnecessary: a simple frequency check upfront determines whether ANY valid arrangement exists at all, and a greedy strategy builds one directly when it does.

What the greedy strategy is: always place the currently most frequent remaining character, unless it was the character just placed, in which case place the next most frequent one instead.

How to access the most frequent character quickly: a max-heap ordered by remaining count.

The core idea: check feasibility with the ceil(n/2) rule, then greedily build the result using a max-heap, always avoiding immediate repeats.

Count character frequencies. If the maximum frequency exceeds ceil(n divided by 2), return an empty string immediately. Otherwise, use a max-heap by frequency: repeatedly pop the most frequent character; if it matches the last character placed, temporarily pop the next one to place instead, then push the first one back. Decrement counts and push back into the heap as long as they remain positive.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: max-heap by count, skip the character just placed

blocks.text: The ceil(n/2) feasibility rule exactly captures whether a character is too frequent to ever be spread out enough. Given that feasibility holds, always placing the most frequent remaining character (deferring to the second most frequent only when the top would repeat the last placed character) provably succeeds in building a valid arrangement, since it keeps every character's count draining as evenly as possible relative to its frequency.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log k), where k is the number of distinct characters, each of n placements triggering an O(log k) heap operation.
Space: O(k) for the heap.

blocks.text: Reorganize String combines a simple feasibility check (the ceil(n/2) rule) with a greedy max-heap construction, always placing the most frequent remaining character while avoiding an immediate repeat.

items: Using n divided by 2 (floor) instead of ceil(n/2) for the feasibility check, which is incorrect for odd-length strings.
Forgetting to temporarily set aside and later restore the top character when it would repeat the last placed one.

blocks.text: Stating the feasibility rule explicitly before describing the greedy construction shows the full reasoning: first determine if an answer can exist, then show how to build one.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "how do you know if it's even possible", think: the most frequent character's count must not exceed ceil(n/2).
If the interviewer says "how do you build a valid arrangement", think: greedily place the most frequent remaining character, using a max-heap, and avoid repeating the previous one.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in factorial time. The optimized feasibility-check-plus-greedy-heap approach runs in O(n log k) time and O(k) space.

items: Pattern: a feasibility check (ceil(n/2) rule) combined with a greedy max-heap construction.

Core Idea: reject immediately if any character is too frequent; otherwise, always place the most frequent remaining character, deferring to the second most frequent only to avoid repeating the last placed one.
Time: factorial for the brute force, O(n log k) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n!) for the brute force, O(k) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: a simple frequency threshold determines feasibility, and a greedy max-heap construction succeeds whenever that threshold is met.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known greedy-plus-heap problem, quick once the feasibility rule and heap-skip logic are recognized.
One line memory trick: ceil(n/2) feasibility check, then max-heap greedy placement, skipping immediate repeats.
